message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"1.1","text":"I, Clement, being a citizen of the Romans, have also been able to live the earliest period of my life with self-control, because from childhood my thought kept the desire within me occupied with dejection and distress. For a thought about death was continually with me—I do not know where it began—repeatedly reminding me that, when I die, I do not exist, and no one will ever make mention of me, since infinite time carries everything belonging to everyone into oblivion. I shall be while not being, knowing those who do not exist, not knowing, not being known, not having come into being, not coming into being. And has the world ever come into being, and before it came into being, what then existed? For if it always existed, it will also exist; but if it came into being, it will also be dissolved. And after its dissolution, what in turn will exist, unless perhaps silence and oblivion? And perhaps there will be something that cannot now be conceived.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"σωφρόνως","chosen":"with self-control","rationale":"Describes restrained or temperate conduct rather than merely prudent thought."},{"source_quote":"ἀπασχολούσης","chosen":"kept occupied","rationale":"Preserves the image of Clement’s thought occupying or diverting his inward desire."},{"source_quote":"πυκνὰς ποιούμενος ὑπομνήσεις","chosen":"repeatedly reminding me","rationale":"The expression depicts the thought as producing frequent reminders."},{"source_quote":"πάντων τὰ πάντα","chosen":"everything belonging to everyone","rationale":"Retains the emphatic combination of the plural possessive and comprehensive object."},{"source_quote":"οὐκ ὄντας εἰδώς","chosen":"knowing those who do not exist","rationale":"Renders the supplied accusative plural as the object of εἰδώς without silently altering the difficult wording."},{"source_quote":"νοῆσαι","chosen":"be conceived","rationale":"Refers to mental conception or apprehension."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"οὐκ ὄντας εἰδώς","issue":"The accusative masculine plural οὐκ ὄντας has no explicit antecedent. Taken substantivally, it yields the unusual and contextually paradoxical wording “knowing those who do not exist.” The supplied reading is retained without emendation.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":true}]},{"reference":"1.2","text":"Constantly pondering these and things like them—I do not know from where—I experienced such painful grief that, having grown pale, I wasted away. And most terrible of all, if I ever resolved to push the concern away as useless, the affliction became still more intense for me. I was troubled at this, not knowing that I had a noble thought as a housemate, one that would become for me the cause of a good immortality, as I later learned by experience and thanked God, the Master of all. For by the thought that distressed me at first, I was compelled to come to the investigation and discovery of realities; and then I counted as wretched those whom at first, through ignorance, I had been in danger of counting blessed.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἀπαύστως ἐνθυμούμενος","chosen":"constantly pondering","rationale":"Conveys both uninterrupted recurrence and inward reflection."},{"source_quote":"ὠχριακότα","chosen":"having grown pale","rationale":"Preserves the physical effect attributed to Clement’s grief."},{"source_quote":"ἀκμαιότερόν","chosen":"still more intense","rationale":"Describes the affliction as becoming stronger or more acute."},{"source_quote":"σύνοικον","chosen":"as a housemate","rationale":"Retains the domestic image of the thought dwelling together with Clement."},{"source_quote":"ἀθανασίας ἀγαθῆς","chosen":"a good immortality","rationale":"Preserves the explicit qualification of immortality as good or beneficial."},{"source_quote":"ζήτησιν καὶ εὕρεσιν","chosen":"investigation and discovery","rationale":"Keeps the paired movement from inquiry to finding."},{"source_quote":"ἐταλάνιζον οὓς τὴν ἀρχὴν διὰ ἄγνοιαν μακαρίζειν ἐκινδύνευον","chosen":"I counted as wretched those whom at first, through ignorance, I had been in danger of counting blessed","rationale":"Preserves the deliberate reversal between regarding people as wretched and regarding them as blessed."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"1.3","text":"Being absorbed in such reasonings from childhood, then, I used to attend the philosophers’ schools in order to learn something certain. And I found nothing else except dismantlings and constructions of doctrines, disputes and rivalries, techniques of syllogisms, and inventions of premises. At one time, to give an example, the view that the soul is immortal prevailed; at another, the view that it is mortal. So whenever an argument that it was immortal prevailed, I rejoiced; but whenever one that it was mortal prevailed, I grieved. Yet I was more disheartened because I could not establish either alternative as certain in my own mind. Nevertheless, I perceived that judgments about the theses are regarded as false or true according to those who defend them, and do not appear as they actually stand with respect to truth. Having therefore at last recognized that a firm grasp does not arise from the theses being defended, but that judgments are pronounced according to those defending them, and reeling still more amid these matters, I consequently groaned from the depth of my soul. For I was neither capable of establishing anything as certain, nor could I shake off concern for such matters, although I wanted to, as I said before; for when I ordered myself more and more often to be still, I do not know how, the thought about such things would enter me unnoticed and with pleasure.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἐφοίτων διατριβάς","chosen":"I used to attend the philosophers’ schools","rationale":"The imperfect indicates habitual attendance, while the setting is one of philosophical instruction."},{"source_quote":"ἀνασκευὰς καὶ κατασκευὰς","chosen":"dismantlings and constructions","rationale":"Preserves the paired destructive and constructive treatment of doctrines."},{"source_quote":"λημμάτων ἐπινοίας","chosen":"inventions of premises","rationale":"λήμματα are propositions or premises adopted for argument, and ἐπινοίας presents them as devised."},{"source_quote":"φέρε λέγειν","chosen":"to give an example","rationale":"The parenthetical expression introduces an illustrative case."},{"source_quote":"ὁπότερον","chosen":"either alternative","rationale":"Refers to the two competing positions concerning the soul’s mortality."},{"source_quote":"δόξαι τῶν ὑποθέσεων","chosen":"judgments about the theses","rationale":"Construes the genitive as identifying the theses about which assessments are made."},{"source_quote":"κατάληψις","chosen":"a firm grasp","rationale":"In this philosophical context, the term denotes secure apprehension rather than merely receiving information."},{"source_quote":"λανθανόντως μεθ᾽ ἡδονῆς","chosen":"unnoticed and with pleasure","rationale":"Retains both the thought’s unnoticed entrance and its expressly pleasurable quality."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἔτι μᾶλλον ἰλιγγίων ἐν τοῖς πράγμασιν.","issue":"As punctuated in the supplied edition, this nominative participial phrase ends a sentence without an expressed finite verb. The translation construes it circumstantially with the following ἐστέναζον while retaining the causal force of διὸ. This treats the printed punctuation interpretively and does not alter the supplied Greek.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"ὅτι ἐμαυτῷ πυκνότερον ἡσυχάζειν ἐπιτάσσοντος","issue":"The genitive participle ἐπιτάσσοντος has no explicit genitive subject, while ἐμαυτῷ is dative. The translation takes Clement as the unexpressed subject and construes ἐμαυτῷ as the person upon whom he enjoins stillness, but the syntax is compressed and unusual.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"1.4","text":"Again, being at a loss, I said to myself, “Why am I laboring in vain? The matter is clear: if, when dead, I do not exist, it is not fitting for me to grieve while I now exist. Therefore I will reserve grieving for that time, when, not existing, I will not grieve. But if, after all, I am something, then grieving now is superfluous for me.” Immediately after this, another thought entered me, for I said, “What if, indeed, because I have not lived devoutly, I am to suffer there something worse than what troubles me now, and according to the accounts of certain philosophers I shall be handed over to Pyriphlegethon and Tartarus, like Sisyphus or Tityus or Ixion or Tantalus, and shall be in Hades, punished for all time?” Then again I countered, saying, “But these things do not exist.” And again I said, “But what if they do?” Since the matter was uncertain, then, I would say, “It is safer for me rather to live devoutly. And how shall I be able, for the sake of what is right, while looking toward an uncertain hope, to master the pleasures of the body? But I have not even been fully assured what right thing is pleasing to God; nor do I know whether the soul is immortal or mortal; nor what reliable argument can be found; nor can I rest from such reasonings.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ματαιοπονῶ","chosen":"am I laboring in vain","rationale":"Preserves the image of expending effort fruitlessly."},{"source_quote":"εἰμί τι","chosen":"I am something","rationale":"Retains the deliberately indefinite τι in Clement’s speculation about existence after death."},{"source_quote":"ἐκ περισσοῦ","chosen":"superfluous","rationale":"Describes the present grief as excessive or unnecessary."},{"source_quote":"Εἰ μήτι γε","chosen":"What if, indeed","rationale":"Introduces an apprehensive exception to Clement’s preceding attempt at reassurance."},{"source_quote":"Πυριφλεγέθοντι καὶ Ταρτάρῳ","chosen":"to Pyriphlegethon and Tartarus","rationale":"Transliterates the named mythological places rather than replacing them with generalized descriptions."},{"source_quote":"τὸν αἰῶνα","chosen":"for all time","rationale":"The accusative phrase expresses the duration of punishment."},{"source_quote":"ἀκινδυνότερόν","chosen":"safer","rationale":"Expresses the comparative absence of risk in choosing a devout life."},{"source_quote":"τοῦ δικαίου χάριν","chosen":"for the sake of what is right","rationale":"The substantivized adjective refers to right conduct without imposing a more specialized theological sense."},{"source_quote":"εἰς ἄδηλον ἐλπίδα ἀφορῶν","chosen":"while looking toward an uncertain hope","rationale":"Preserves both the uncertainty of the hope and the image of directing one’s attention toward it."},{"source_quote":"πεπληροφόρημαι","chosen":"I have not even been fully assured","rationale":"The perfect verb itself conveys settled or full assurance; “fully” is not an added intensifier."},{"source_quote":"λόγος βέβαιος","chosen":"reliable argument","rationale":"In this philosophical setting λόγος can denote a reasoned account or argument, while βέβαιος marks it as dependable."}],"source_issues":[]}]}
